extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, narratologists, advanced students of narrative theory, and critics analyzing narrative temporality
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and evaluating a narrative's temporal organization and pacing (order, duration, frequency) using Genette's concepts (anachronies, anisochronies, syllepsis, the four narrative movements, etc.). Useful for close readings, comparative analysis, and creative-writing craft studies focused on time and tempo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achrony (dateless event)
rubrics_metrics.description: An event deprived of every temporal connection, which the analyst must take to be dateless and ageless: an achrony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such events cannot be temporally located by inference from content. Example: an isolated anecdote with no temporal markers; the analyst should recognize its status as achronal rather than force a chronological placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronies (analepses and prolepses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrospective and anticipatory displacements of narrative order: analepses (retrospection) and prolepses (anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify these as departures from chronological (diegetic) order. Use them to map how the narrative rearranges events in telling; they are one constitutive feature of narrative temporality but not the whole story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllepsis (grouping by kinship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Groupings of events governed by a kinship relation (spatial, temporal, thematic, or other) rather than strict chronological succession; Genette names these 'syllepses'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types: geographic syllepsis (voyage narratives grouped by stops), thematic syllepsis (episodic insertions justified by analogy/contrast), iterative narrative as a variety. Use syllepsis to explain non-chronological sequencing grounded in spatial or thematic relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic ordering (spatially governed succession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative order governed by the itinerary or spatial sequence of locations rather than by the temporal sequence of events (e.g., train stops that evoke anecdotes in that order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when succession depends on location or the narrator's associative order (sites evoking anecdotes) rather than event chronology. Beware naive conflation of syntagmatic order with story-time order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative autonomy from story chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative's capacity to disengage its arrangement from dependence (or inverse dependence) on the chronological sequence of the story it tells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a text, assess how much the narrative order reflects associative, spatial, thematic, or rhythmic principles instead of diegetic chronology. Example: grouping childhood episodes by thematic affinity regardless of their chronological order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anisochronies (distortions of speed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distortions in narrative speed (variations in rate) that contribute to emancipation from narrative temporality as much as transgressions of chronological order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze accelerations and slowdowns (macroscopic units preferred). Look for how speed variation structures emphasis, rhythm, and perceived importance of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of measuring narrative duration
rubrics_metrics.description: No precise measure exists for 'narrative duration' because reading time varies; unlike film or music, there's no normal speed of execution to compare against story time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claims that rely on an exact equality between narrative length and story duration. Any measurement must be approximate and relative; prefer macroscopic, statistical approximations over fine-grained temporal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isochrony as theoretical reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Isochronous narrative: hypothetical reference zero defined as unchanging speed where the relationship (duration-of-story)/(length-of-narrative) remains steady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use isochrony only as an abstract benchmark—Genette notes such narratives don't exist in practice. Useful for comparative thinking about departures from steadiness (i.e., rhythm effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Macroscopic unit analysis (large syntagmatic categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because diegetic time is rarely precisely indicated, analysis of duration/tempo should be done at the macroscopic level of large narrative units (the 'large syntagmatic category').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define large articulations by important temporal and/or spatial breaks. Establish approximate internal chronology for each unit to estimate story-time covered. Provide examples (Genette's eleven units for Proust's Recherche).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demarcation criterion for narrative units
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt significant temporal and/or spatial breaks as the demarcating criterion to establish narrative units for rhythm and duration analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette offers an operational (not sacrosanct) carving: list units bounded by clear breaks (e.g., Combray, Un amour de Swann, Balbec I/II). Use these to compute rough page-to-story-time ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve external vs internal chronology conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of and account for contradictions between external/historical chronologies and the work's internal chronology when establishing story time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When external references (historical events) contradict internal sequencing, analysts may need to discard problematic external series or form a provisional internal chronology anchored to robust internal guide marks (e.g., Dreyfus affair, The War). Document uncertainties and their effect on duration estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four canonical narrative movements (tempo forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary tradition selects four basic relationships of story-time to narrative-time: descriptive pause, scene, summary, and ellipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these canonical forms to classify narrative segments. Genette gives schematic formulas: descriptive_pause NT = n, ST = 0; scene NT = ST; summary NT < ST; ellipsis NT = 0, ST = n. They function as the primary toolkit for analyzing narrative tempo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene (equality of narrative and story time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene conventionally realizes the equality between narrative section and fictive section (NT = ST), often exemplified by dialogue or uninterrupted depiction of an event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify scenes where the text attempts to reproduce the event's duration; note limitations (it doesn't restore exact speech rhythms or gaps). Scenes are useful as conventional markers but not rigorous temporal measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary (variable, intermediate tempo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary is a form with variable tempo that covers the range between scene and ellipsis (NT < ST), used to compress several days, months, or years into shorter narrative space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize classical summaries (e.g., Don Quixote example) and contrast with Proust's near-absence of traditional summary. Summaries often serve to provide connective tissue between scenes or to sketch past life rapidly; in retrospection they commonly convey past life efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis (narrative omission of story duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipsis is the absence of narrative time corresponding to some duration in the story (NT = 0, ST = n): sections of story omitted from the narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when the narrative jumps over spans of story-time without telling them. Ellipses function to compress or omit periods (e.g., 'many years passed') and can border on acceleration or summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive pause (narrative time with no diegetic duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive pause: a narrative section corresponds to no diegetic duration (NT = n, ST = 0); the narrative dwells on description rather than action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between description and descriptive pause: not every description is a pause (some descriptions are diegetic and iterative). Also distinguish author's intrusions (non-diegetic commentary) from descriptive pauses which remain part of the diegetic universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of NT>ST canonical form (no slow-motion scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an asymmetry: literary tradition lacks a canonical form where narrative time systematically exceeds story time (NT > ST) — a 'scene in slow motion' is not a canonical, widely actualized form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While experiments exist (e.g., very long textual stretches for short events), Genette treats such slow-motion as exceptional or achieved by insertions, not a standard category. Analysts should treat apparent 'slow-motion' as scene plus extranarrative insertions or descriptive pauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative narrative as a tempo/structural principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterative narrative (repetition/series) often governs descriptions or accounts that are not tied to a specific moment and thus do not function as pauses; iterative elements are a variety of syllepsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a description or account recurs across analogous moments (e.g., repeated images, rooms), count it as iterative; it may accelerate rather than slow the narrative. Use this to explain passages that seem descriptive but serve a repeated/diachronic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing narrative evolution in tempo (e.g., Proustian case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate internal evolution of narrative tempo across a work: e.g., Genette finds a 'gradual slowing down' through increasingly long scenes covering short story-times combined with more massive ellipses—an increasing discontinuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map page-to-story-time ratios across units to observe trends (e.g., later volumes with enormous scenes separated by long gaps). Consider publication, compositional history, and authorial intent as possible explanations but focus analysis on the structural temporal effects.
